gold.rationale: The issue has an empty body and a title with no substantive content ('liteLLM'). There is no information about what the user wants, whether it's a bug, question, or feature. This is an unintelligible/empty issue with no actionable information, so per rules it defaults to 'question' category with needs_human set to true due to insufficient information.

This is a well-documented, reproducible bug: nullable columns in composite unique constraints combined with inconsistent NULL/empty-string handling between the `where` and `create` payloads in `_update_daily_spend` cause duplicate physical rows across six daily-spend tables. This affects the shared core spend-tracking path used by all providers/deployments, leading to database CPU exhaustion and fragmented spend reporting in production. It matches "bug" category (behavior violates documented/intended uniqueness contract). Given it affects the shared core path across six tables and causes severe operational impact (CPU exhaustion, multi-GB bloat) with no stated workaround, and shared-core-path issues raise urgency one level, this warrants P1. It needs human review because it's a significant correctness/performance issue spanning schema changes, backfill strategy, and multiple tables — a judgement call on the fix approach (schema migration vs. code fix) is required before routing.

This is a credential exposure issue: API keys (and potentially proxy master/virtual keys) are printed unredacted to stdout via litellm/utils.py::print_verbose, an inconsistency with the already-redacted _logging.py path. This is a plausible exploit path (log collectors capturing secrets in plaintext), so per the rules it takes precedence as security regardless of it being framed as a bug. It affects the shared core logging path used across all providers when set_verbose/debug logging is enabled, which is a widely used path, but has a straightforward workaround (avoid set_verbose=True, or disable via LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS is unrelated) - actually there's no real workaround to avoid the leak other than not using verbose mode, but disabling verbose mode is itself a workaround. Given it's a credential leak affecting many users' logs when debug/verbose mode is enabled (common in production troubleshooting), and no simple fix without code change, this warrants P1. Security issues always need human judgement/review before routing.

This is a well-documented feature request to add lock_timeout/statement_timeout configuration to the partition management DDL path in SpendLogs cleanup, to prevent a real production outage caused by DDL blocking on locks held by routine Postgres maintenance (VACUUM). While it's framed as caused by a production incident, the ask itself is a new capability (exposing timeout settings) that doesn't exist yet — this is a feature, not a bug in existing documented behavior. The issue is a single detailed report from one reporter with no corroboration from other users, but it does describe a real outage-causing scenario affecting the shared SpendLogs partition management path used by all proxy DB users, which is a widely-used/core path. Per rules, feature requests default to P3, promoted to P2 on evidenced demand (widely-used provider or shared core path affected) — since SpendLogs partition management is core shared logic affecting many proxy deployments with Postgres, this qualifies for the "shared core path affected" raise. No regression modifier applies (this behavior always lacked timeouts). No workaround-lower modifier needed. This requires product-direction judgement (should timeouts be exposed as configurable settings, what defaults) so a maintainer should review before routing/implementation.

The issue has no title content beyond a greeting and an empty body. There is no information to determine what the reporter needs, no reproduction, no question, no feature request—nothing actionable. Per the rules, an empty or unintelligible issue defaults to 'question' category, and the lack of information means a maintainer must look at it before it can be routed or closed.

This is a clear regression: LiteLLM v1.90.0 introduced forwarding of `strict`/`additionalProperties` to Bedrock Converse for Claude models without proper model-specific handling, causing 400 errors and hanging requests (504 timeouts) for multiple widely-used Claude models (Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5) via Bedrock, a core/shared provider path. There's already a related issue and PR open for one of the affected models, corroborating demand and confirming this is a known regression affecting the shared Bedrock tool-calling path. This is a functional bug (wrong behavior vs. documented/expected behavior, causing errors and hangs), not a docs or feature issue. Given it's a regression affecting a widely-used provider path (Bedrock Converse + multiple Claude models) with no full workaround (partial workaround only for one model via a client-side hook), this warrants high urgency. Base severity is P1 (major provider path broken, painful workaround exists for one case only) and regression modifier would push to P0, but workaround existing lowers it back down partially - however already many providers/models affected pushes it up. Given the severity (500s, hangs, timeouts) affecting multiple Claude models via Bedrock but a workaround exists (prepare_tools hook setting strict=False), I'll set urgency to P1 due to regression + shared core path affected, tempered by partial workaround. This requires maintainer judgement to reconcile multiple related PRs/issues and confirm the fix scope across models, so needs_human=true.

This is a clearly reproduced regression introduced in v1.93.0: a new get_supported_event_hooks activation combined with a metadata sanitization change causes a None.get() AttributeError, crashing every /v1/batches create call when a post_call Model Armor guardrail is active. The Vertex batch job is created but the client never gets a response, leaving orphan jobs and no correlation ID header. This affects a widely-used provider path (vertex_ai batches) combined with a common guardrail feature, is a regression from a prior working version, and has clear reproduction steps and root-cause analysis pointing to exact code lines. It's a bug, not a feature or question, since documented/expected behavior (successful batch creation returning to caller) is violated. Given it's a regression breaking a core proxy endpoint for any user combining post_call guardrails, severity is high (P1), raised from baseline due to regression modifier, but not P0 since no data loss/security issue and vertex batches specifically. No workaround stated, so no downgrade. Because this is a well-documented regression with exact code pointers, though it involves a P1-level severity requiring reproduction confirmation and judgement on fix scope (metadata None-safety across guardrails), a maintainer should review to confirm scope of fix (just this line vs broader safety net for other guardrails).

This is an outreach/notification from a third-party benchmark site asking LiteLLM maintainers to review their gateway.sh configuration for fairness. It's not a bug report, feature request, or documentation issue about LiteLLM's own docs/code. It doesn't ask "how to do something" in the sense of using the library, but it is a request for maintainer attention/validation of an external benchmark setup, which requires human judgement (product/community decision on whether to engage, verify config correctness, etc.). It best fits "question" category since no actual code misbehavior is claimed, just a request for review. Urgency is low since there's no functional impact on users; it's a courtesy check-in with optional asks. Needs human because it requires maintainer judgement on whether the benchmark config is accurate/fair, which is a domain-specific validation task, not something that can be auto-routed.

This is a request for new functionality (adding Nano-GPT to the UI provider dropdown) that already exists as a documented provider but isn't selectable in the UI. This is a well-specified, single-user feature request without evidenced demand from multiple users. It falls under 'feature' category since it's about adding new UI support that doesn't currently exist. Since it's a single requester with no corroboration, it defaults to P3 despite being well-argued. It's a clear, well-specified feature request that can be routed to the UI/provider team without further clarification needed.

The reporter describes existing documented behavior (Voxtral is only supported via audio_transcription mode, not chat completions) and requests either surfacing it in /v1/models or clarifying docs. This is a mix of a minor bug/feature (models endpoint not listing audio models with mode metadata) and a docs improvement request. Since the code behaves as designed (Voxtral works via audio_transcription mode) but the discoverability via /v1/models is missing and docs could be clearer, this is best categorized as docs/feature improvement. Given the primary ask is about model listing behavior not matching expectations, and it's a single reporter's request without evidence of widespread demand, treat as a feature-ish/docs enhancement rather than a critical bug. It's a narrow, well-specified issue that doesn't need maintainer judgement on scope - it can be routed as a docs/feature clarification. Urgency low since there's a workaround (manual model_list config) and it's a single reporter.

This is a request to add a new provider (WaveSpeed.ai) for both LLM inference and media generation, which does not currently exist in LiteLLM. This is clearly a feature request for new provider support. There's no evidence of multiple users requesting this (single requester, detailed write-up but no corroboration), so per the rules it defaults to P3 despite the thorough justification. It is a well-specified feature request that can be queued for the provider-integration backlog without needing a maintainer conversation first to clarify scope, though a product-direction call on whether to support a new media-generation type API might be warranted. Given the complexity (two distinct APIs: chat completions and async media generation) and the product-direction nature of adding a wholly new provider type (prediction-based media API differs from existing patterns), a maintainer should weigh in before implementation.

This is a well-specified request for new functionality (recurring access schedules) that does not currently exist in virtual key permissions. It's a feature request rather than a bug, since existing behavior works as documented—there's simply no such capability yet. There is no evidence of demand beyond the single requester (no other users or maintainers cited), so per rules it defaults to P3 despite the detailed write-up. It is well-specified enough (concrete JSON schema, validation points, enforcement location, test plan) that it could be queued as a feature without a maintainer conversation, though the decision of whether to build this is a product-direction call best left to a maintainer to confirm before implementation.

The issue has no meaningful title or body—just "lol" with an empty body. There's no information to determine what the reporter is asking about, reporting, or requesting. This is unintelligible/near-empty content, which per the rules defaults to 'question' category, and requires human attention due to insufficient information to route it anywhere meaningful.

The reported behavior violates the documented Anthropic Messages spec contract: stop_reason must be "tool_use" when a tool_use block is present, and streaming should not emit a spurious empty text block. The non-streaming path behaves correctly, confirming this is a code defect in the streaming translation logic specific to ollama_chat -> Anthropic /v1/messages adapter, not a docs issue or a question. This is a clear bug with detailed, deterministic reproduction steps. It affects a specific but widely-used integration path (streaming tool calls via Anthropic-compatible clients like Claude Code) — this breaks all tool-calling use cases over the streaming Anthropic-messages transport for ollama_chat models, and likely other providers using the same streaming translation code, since it's about the shared Anthropic streaming adapter logic. No workaround is stated (switching off streaming is a functional workaround, but that defeats the purpose of streaming for many production copilot/agent uses). Given the impact -- tool calls silently fail closed for any tool-capable streaming request via this transport -- this is significant, though scoped to one code path (Anthropic streaming translation with tool use), not "most users on a current release broken" universally. I'll set urgency P1 given it breaks a major feature (tool calling for streaming) for users going through this integration, with reproduction steps provided. It's a clear, well-specified bug report with clear repro and expected output, so a maintainer doesn't need to triage/investigate further before routing it to the owning module (though given severity, I'd still flag needs_human due to P1 threshold in the rules).

This is a detailed, well-researched issue containing multiple distinct problems: (1) a concrete bug where falsy-zero check causes rate-limit gauges to silently drop 0 values, masking real quota exhaustion (a correctness bug in the prometheus exporter's alerting path); (2) a feature request to add a `region` dimension to metrics; (3) a feature request to add `call_type` dimension; (4) an open question about image generation metric coverage across providers. Per the rules, when multiple distinct problems are bundled together, the primary actionable and highest-severity item should drive classification. Problem 1 is a clear bug with reproduction (before/after behavior described, PR #29214 referenced) affecting alerting/observability correctness — this is the most severe and concrete claim, so category = bug. The other problems are feature requests (region/call_type labels) referencing precedent PR #32126, showing some evidenced demand shape but still essentially a single reporter's proposal - however this affects prometheus metrics used broadly for cost/latency monitoring across multiple providers, and the bug about zero-value gauges affects rate-limit alerting broken silently in production which impacts monitoring reliability for exporter users generally, though it's a narrower monitoring path with a workaround already found (patched build) - stated workaround lowers severity one level. Given it's a monitoring gauge issue (not a full outage-causing bug, workaround already applied by reporter), and affects a subset of users who use rate-limit gauges/alerting, I set urgency P2 (narrower path affected, workaround exists onset P1->P2). Since this bundles multiple distinct problems (4 separate issues) and requires maintainer judgement to decide which of the feature-shaped asks to accept and reproduce the zero-gauge bug, needs_human = true.

The code behaves as intended (pooling now works correctly for REDIS_URL); the documentation is simply outdated, citing a performance issue that has since been fixed. The issue proposes a specific, well-reasoned doc update (drop performance claim, add configuration caveat about REDIS_PASSWORD/options not being forwarded outside the URL). This is a clear docs issue, not a bug, since there's no code misbehavior claimed—only a documentation staleness problem. It's low urgency (cosmetic/doc accuracy), and the suggested fix is well-specified enough to route directly without maintainer discussion.

This is a clear bug: the MCP DCR bridge forwards the OAuth token_type verbatim without canonicalizing case, causing strict providers to reject the Authorization header with HTTP 401. This violates RFC 6749's case-insensitivity expectation for token_type and results in zero tools being returned - a functional break for a subset of providers that strictly enforce scheme casing. The reporter provided a clear reproduction, root cause, and even a minimal patch, so this can be routed directly to the owning module without further discussion. It affects only providers that strictly validate the Authorization scheme casing (a subset, not all providers), and a workaround might not be readily available to end users (they can't control upstream provider strictness), but it's not a security vulnerability, not a documentation issue, and not a feature request - it's a clear functional bug in the bridge_credentials module. Since it's narrowly scoped to providers with strict casing checks, and a fix is trivial and well-specified, this fits P2 (narrower path broken, subset affected). No regression indicated (this seems to be a first-time implementation issue in the DCR bridge, not a working feature that broke), so no raise. No workaround stated by reporter for end users, so no lower. Given the clear reproduction, fix, and specificity, needs_human can be false - this is routable without discussion.

This is a well-specified feature request proposing new configuration (session_key_fallback), fallback resolution logic, and observability improvements for the auto router when session_id is absent. No code is currently broken relative to documented behavior — the docs state this is the current behavior, so it's not a bug. It's a single requester (no corroboration of demand from multiple users, though solid reasoning), so per rules it defaults to P3 despite being detailed and well-argued. It touches the shared core routing path (session_affinity/adaptive), but the "many providers or shared core path affected" modifier is meant for widespread breakage, not a proposed enhancement — and a detailed write-up alone isn't evidence of demand. This is a product-direction call (whether to add fallback key derivation, security-sensitive scoping design) that a maintainer should weigh in on before queuing, so needs_human should be true despite feature-not-bug classification.

The SAP provider fails to preserve cache_control markers on message content, which is documented/expected behavior consistent with Anthropic's prompt-caching API and with litellm's own anthropic provider. This is a functional gap causing wrong behavior (cost/caching not activating) rather than a missing feature from scratch — the provider already handles messages/content but silently drops a field, leading to incorrect cost/token accounting (cache_read/cache_creation always 0). This matches the "bug" category per the rules ("incorrect cost or token accounting" is explicitly called out as a bug). It affects a narrower path (SAP provider users routing Anthropic models), so not most users of the library, but it's a real functional defect with a clear reproduction. No workaround is mentioned other than not using caching, so it stays at P2 given it's a subset of users (SAP provider only) affected, with a clear repro provided. It does not rise to P1 since SAP provider is a narrow/less widely used path, not the shared core path. Given the clear reproduction and well-scoped nature, a maintainer could route this without deep discussion, but since it involves a design/API extension (adding cache_control field support across multiple models to reach parity) and affects a specific provider integration, some judgement on scope might be needed, but the report is well-specified and reproducible enough to route directly to the SAP owning module.

This is a genuine bug: documented/expected behavior (buffered spend gets flushed and persisted, as shown by the analogous enterprise billing flush) is violated — in-memory spend buffers (update_spend, update_daily_tag_spend) are silently dropped on shutdown, causing billing/spend data loss on every worker recycle or SIGTERM. This affects the shared spend-tracking path used by virtually all proxy deployments with a DB configured, and happens on every restart (common operational event: rolling deploys, autoscaling, MAX_REQUESTS_BEFORE_RESTART), with no workaround mentioned. Data loss of billing-relevant records on a widely used core path is severe — this qualifies for P0 given "data loss" and "broken for most users on current release" criteria, but there is a workaround-like mitigation (avoid restarts) that isn't really practical, so treat as P1 given it's an edge/timing-window issue (only rows since last batch interval) rather than total breakage, but it affects the shared core path for essentially all proxy+DB users. Given the shared-core-path modifier (raise one level) and no workaround, I'll set to P0 since it's data loss affecting billing accuracy for most proxy users. Actually reflecting further: impact is bounded to a small window of rows per restart, not to the majority of requests being broken — so P1 fits better (major feature/shared core path broken, painful but partial impact, no workaround). This requires maintainer judgement to confirm impact and decide on the flush fix, so needs_human=true.

This is a well-documented data-integrity bug: spend log rows are popped from the in-memory queue before the DB write is awaited, and cancellation (via scheduler shutdown or an unmanaged monitor task) results in silent, permanent loss of spend rows with no requeue/shielding. The code does not behave as documented/expected (spend should be durably persisted), qualifying as a bug rather than a feature or docs issue. It's not security since there's no attacker-controlled exploit path—only a shutdown-timing race. This affects the shared spend-logging path used by all proxy deployments with DB-backed spend tracking, which is a core/widely-used path, and results in silent data loss (billing-adjacent) with no workaround (the reporter explicitly showed the "obvious fixes" don't work). That warrants raising urgency above baseline; given it's data loss on a core path affecting most DB-enabled proxy deployments during any restart/SIGTERM, it fits P0/P1. Since it's not exploitable and requires a shutdown timing rather than constant breakage, and there's no simple workaround, but it does affect nearly all users with spend tracking on any restart — treat as P1 (major, core-path broken across restarts) rather than P0. This requires maintainer judgement: the issue explicitly explains why naive fixes (shield alone, requeue alone) don't work and require coordinated changes across several modules (idempotency in guardrail usage tracking, shielding, disconnect ordering) — a design/architecture decision, so needs_human = true.

This is a clear bug: budget_limits window resets are delayed by the timezone offset due to incorrect timezone handling (stripping tzinfo without converting to UTC first) in ResetBudgetJob._reset_expired_window(). The reporter has provided a precise root cause, code diff fix, and detailed reproduction steps with logs. This affects any proxy deployment using a non-UTC timezone with budget_limits, causing keys to remain incorrectly rate-limited (429) for up to the timezone offset duration. This is a functional correctness bug affecting a subset of users (those using non-UTC timezones with budget_limits, a feature added relatively recently in v1.83.10). A workaround might be to use UTC timezone, which would lower the severity. Given the narrow scope (only affects budget_limits with non-UTC timezone, not budget_duration) and workaround availability (set timezone to UTC), this is P2 rather than P1. Since the report is detailed, well-reproduced, with root cause and fix already identified, this can be routed directly without maintainer discussion — needs_human is false.

This is a well-documented feature request for an escape hatch/configuration option to opt out of the automatic responseJsonSchema behavior for Vertex AI Gemini 2.x+ models, in favor of native responseSchema. The reporter explicitly states "No default-behavior change is proposed — just an escape hatch," framing this as a new capability rather than fixing broken documented behavior. While the issue provides strong evidence of quality degradation from the current hardcoded behavior, the ask is for a new configurable parameter/setting that doesn't exist today, which is a feature request rather than a bug report against documented behavior.

The request shows evidenced demand: it cites two external prior-art issues (google/adk-python#4367 experiencing the same problem, langchain-ai/langchain-google#1078 treating this as an explicit user choice), extensive empirical data across multiple documents/runs, and affects a widely-used provider (Vertex AI Gemini, a major provider) and the shared structured-output code path. This satisfies the "evidenced demand" and "widely-used provider affected" criteria, justifying P2 (feature default P3, promoted due to evidenced demand and shared core path impact for Vertex AI).

Since this is a well-specified feature request (proposes two concrete API shapes) that only needs to be queued/prioritized by maintainers for implementation, it doesn't require a judgement call on whether to build vs not — though because it touches structured output behavior broadly (which could affect other Vertex users depending on responseJsonSchema behavior) and involves weighing product direction (which mechanism to expose), maintainer input is warranted before implementation begins.

This is a clear, well-documented bug: streaming /v1/messages requests routed through the OpenAI Responses-API bridge silently drop all success callbacks due to a mistagged call_type causing a validation error that kills the fire-and-forget logging task. This is a data-loss issue affecting cost/spend tracking for a widely-used provider (OpenAI) and a shared code path (logging), with no client-visible symptom and no workaround. It behaves differently from expected/documented behavior (cost tracking should work), so it's a bug, not docs/question/feature. Given silent loss of spend records at scale (~30k/day) for a major provider with no workaround, this qualifies as P0 per rules (data loss, broken for many users on current release, no workaround) — though it could arguably be P1 since it's "only" logging that's broken not the actual request. However the rules explicitly list "data loss" as a P0 criterion, and lost cost/spend records constitute data loss for observability purposes affecting many users with no workaround. Given the severity and detailed root-cause analysis, but it does need human judgement to confirm the exact reproduction/root cause claims and decide the fix approach, so needs_human=true.

A live, mutable dict (model_call_details) is embedded by reference into a guardrail payload and concurrently mutated by another thread during JSON serialization, causing RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. This is a clear code defect causing crashes/500s or silently skipped scans - a bug, not a security issue (no exploit path, just a race condition) and not a docs issue since behavior violates expectations. This affects only users of the Noma v2 guardrail (a narrower path), with a documented reproduction and a specific proposed fix. Since it's narrower (single guardrail integration) rather than a widely-used provider or core path, it doesn't warrant P1, but the crash can cause 500s with no workaround for those affected, so P2 is appropriate. The issue includes a clear reproduction and a well-specified fix (mirroring an already-accepted fix pattern in #34720), so it can be routed directly without further maintainer discussion.

The reporter identifies that the docs for the docker quick start guide are incomplete regarding a pure config-based setup without postgres, and offers to contribute a docker-compose.yml example via PR. The code behaves as intended; this is purely a documentation gap/clarity issue, not a bug. It's a well-specified, low-effort contribution that can be routed without maintainer discussion - it's essentially asking permission to open a PR for docs improvement. No demand signal beyond the reporter, and it's cosmetic/minor in nature.

This is a well-specified request for a new capability (native multi-tenancy/tenant isolation for vector storage and RAG endpoints) that does not currently exist in LiteLLM Proxy. No existing behavior is broken; this is purely additive functionality with a detailed proposed config schema. Per the rules, feature requests default to P3 unless there's evidenced demand (multiple requesters, maintainer signal, or wide provider/core impact). This issue is from a single requester with a detailed write-up but no corroborating demand from others — a detailed write-up alone does not count as demand. While it does touch multiple providers (OpenSearch, Vertex AI, Azure AI Search, etc.), this is a proposal for a brand-new cross-cutting capability rather than a fix affecting many providers' existing functionality, so I will not promote to P2 solely on this basis absent other evidence of demand. This is a product-direction decision (whether to build a whole new multi-tenancy subsystem) requiring maintainer judgement, so needs_human is true.

The documented contract is that keys explicitly listed in callback_settings.otel.baggage_metadata_keys should be stamped onto LLM-call spans regardless of whether the span was created at pre-call boundary or deferred. The code violates this contract: _close_llm_call() skips applying the allowlist for boundary-born spans, causing inconsistent, allowlist-violating behavior and breaking downstream vendor mappers like Langfuse. This is a clear code defect against intended/documented behavior, so it's a bug, not a docs issue. It affects the common path (OTel v2 pre-call span creation is the default flow), is a narrow-ish but real correctness/integration issue affecting metadata propagation for many users using otel + langfuse integration, but there's a workaround (using deferred span creation, or not relying on that specific metadata path) and it's not causing crashes or breaking most users outright — it's a subset of users using specific config. I'll rate it P2: narrower path broken, workaround-ish exists (deferred path behaves differently, or not using boundary-fast path), affects OTel + Langfuse users specifically. Given it touches shared core code path (metadata module) but only affects metadata stamping not core functionality, P2 fits best absent evidence of very widespread impact. It has a clear reproduction and specific fix suggestion, so it can be routed without maintainer conversation — needs_human is false since this is a well-described bug with reproduction steps and even a suggested fix.

This is a clear regression: internal rate-limiter metadata leaks into the upstream-visible `metadata` field for /v1/responses requests, causing OpenAI-compatible backends to reject valid requests with HTTP 400. This is a functional bug (not security-sensitive, no exploit path) that violates expected behavior and was introduced by a prior PR (#32711), making it a regression from a previously working state. It affects any user who applies RPM/TPM/max-parallel-request limits to keys/users/teams when using the Responses API against backends that reject unknown metadata — a fairly broad and commonly configured feature (rate limiting) combined with a specific API path (Responses), so impact is meaningful but not "most users." A workaround exists (`additional_drop_params: [metadata]`), which would normally lower severity, but the regression modifier raises it back up. Given clear reproduction steps, root cause identified with exact line references, and clear expected vs actual behavior, this can be routed directly without maintainer discussion — it's a well-scoped, reproducible bug fix.

This is a well-specified request to add a new opt-in configuration option (strict authentication mode) for the marketplace endpoint. It explicitly proposes new behavior that does not exist today (defaulting to false, opt-in), making it a feature request rather than a bug — the current behavior is by design (public endpoint), and the issue seeks new functionality. It references a related security discussion but frames it as a feature to add optional stricter auth, not reporting an active exploit being used against them; it's a proactive hardening feature. Since it's a single requester without evidence of multiple users demanding this, though it references an unresolved security review comment on a PR, suggesting maintainer awareness/intent, which could count as signal of demand. Given the connection to a security review thread and the sensitivity of exposing internal metadata, this needs a maintainer's judgement call on whether to implement, and the security implications need evaluation despite being filed as a feature. This is a product-direction decision requiring human review before routing.

This is a well-specified feature request identifying a parity gap between /v1/messages and /v1/chat/completions regarding fallback transparency. The reporter proposes a concrete design and offers to contribute a PR. It's a single reporter with no corroborated evidence of broader demand (though it affects gateway/fallback users, a legitimate but narrower use case). This is a feature (new capability - exposing served model info that doesn't currently exist), not a bug, since current behavior (echoing requested model) is arguably by design and not violating documented behavior. Since it's a feature request without evidenced multi-party demand, default to P3, though the shared-core-path argument could bump it, but this is specific to /v1/messages fallback scenario, not a widely-used core path affecting most users. Needs human judgement: this requires a product-direction decision on API design (headers-only vs. opt-in body.model change) and whether to accept the contribution — a classic maintainer call.

This is a security-relevant safety bypass: post_call guardrails (content moderation/blocking) are silently skipped on /v1/messages streaming, allowing blocked content to reach clients while the audit log falsely records a successful scan. This is effectively a guardrail bypass / safety-filter bypass, which has security implications (false sense of protection, potential for harmful/blocked content leakage), but it's fundamentally a functional defect in a security control rather than a classic vulnerability like injection or credential exposure. Given the guidance that security takes precedence when there's a plausible exploit path, and here the "exploit" is trivially bypassing a moderation/guardrail control via a documented endpoint, this leans toward security. However, it's also arguably a core bug in a widely-used feature (guardrails on streaming). Given the silent failure with false audit logging (data integrity issue) and the fact that guardrails are a safety/security mechanism, I'll classify as security due to the bypass nature and silent failure with false success reporting, which is a serious issue affecting trust and safety controls.

This affects a widely-used provider path (Anthropic /v1/messages) and the shared guardrail core path, with no workaround mentioned (other than not using /v1/messages streaming with guardrails). This is a significant, exploitable gap in security controls for many users using Anthropic streaming with guardrails, warranting high urgency. Since it's a security-related issue with a plausible "exploit" (bypassing content moderation) and affects the shared guardrail core path, I'll set urgency to P1 (major feature broken - guardrails broken for a widely used provider/endpoint, silent failure, no workaround stated other than avoiding streaming). Security issues and P1s require human judgement per rules, and this needs reproduction/confirmation and product-direction decisions about how to handle guardrails for unsupported formats (fail closed policy), so needs_human = true.

This is a feature request for health-aware multi-backend routing/failover for Anthropic models across direct API, Bedrock, and Vertex AI. The behavior does not currently exist, so it falls under "feature". There's a prior PR draft from a single requester, but no evidence of broader demand from multiple users or maintainer signal of intent - it's a single author proposing to re-open their own closed PR. Per the rules, feature requests default to P3 unless there's evidenced demand (multiple people asking, maintainer intent, or a widely-used provider/shared core path affected). While Anthropic and Bedrock are widely used providers, this is a specific routing feature request, not a broken shared path - it's asking whether the project wants to build this. Since it's a single requester with no corroboration, it stays at P3. This requires a product-direction judgment call by a maintainer (whether to accept this architectural feature and re-open the PR), so needs_human should be true.

A malformed tool_calls arguments JSON causes a non-retryable, pre-network parsing error to be misclassified as a retryable APIConnectionError. Combined with an unbounded/cyclic fallback graph walked without cycle detection, this produces tens of thousands of retries in seconds, saturating the event loop, flooding logs, starving health checks, and causing the pod to be OOM/CPU-killed (exit 137). This is a legitimate availability-impacting bug: incorrect error classification + missing cycle detection in retry/fallback logic causing resource exhaustion and denial of service triggerable by a single unprivileged client request with no large payload or misconfiguration beyond normal usage. While it has DoS-like characteristics, it stems from a functional defect (wrong exception mapping + missing loop-detection) rather than an exploit of an auth/injection/credential path, so 'bug' is the more precise category per the taxonomy (transformation/retry bugs are explicitly bug-category), though the security angle is real and should be flagged for maintainer judgement. Severity: broken for any user who sends a request with malformed tool_call arguments, no workaround except client-side sanitization, causes full replica outage, self-amplifying across replicas — this meets P0 criteria (broken for most users of the affected path, effectively data-loss/availability outage, no real workaround, current release affected). needs_human=true because this requires maintainer judgement on both the security/DoS classification and the retry-classification bug, and touches multiple subsystems (exception mapping, router fallback graph, retry logic) — a judgement call on how to fix cycle detection and reclassify errors, not something to auto-route.

The Admin UI session cookie embeds the user's actual proxy master/admin key in a JWT claim, and the cookie lacks HttpOnly, exposing a full-privilege key to any script running on the page (XSS or malicious extension) and allowing it to be used outside the browser entirely. Additionally, logout does not revoke the key server-side, so a leaked/copied key remains valid for its full lifetime. This is a credential exposure / unsafe default with a clear, plausible exploit path (script reads document.cookie, extracts a live sk- key, uses it directly against the API to mint new keys or read spend), which meets the security category bar and takes precedence over bug framing. It affects the shared UI/auth path used by all proxy admins and SSO users, has no workaround for the underlying design flaw (aside from not using the UI), and there is a data/credential exposure risk with no mitigation — this warrants P0. Given it's a security issue, needs_human must be true for a maintainer to assess and validate the proposed fix (opaque session token direction) even though the reporter offers a PR.

Given the shared core path is affected and this misleads users about a core feature (structured outputs) with a silent failure mode, this deserves elevated urgency. There is a workaround (use text.format directly), which would normally lower severity, but the silent failure and lack of error, plus impact on structured-output reliability for any provider under Responses API, keeps it fairly serious. I'll set P1 given it's a correctness bug on a shared/core path (silent misbehavior affecting structured output for widely-used provider openai, no warning), but a workaround exists so I will not go to P0. It causes skipped shutdown steps including billing metrics flush (data loss) and langfuse flush for any user running Redis cluster mode - a widely used deployment pattern (e.g., ElastiCache Serverless is always cluster mode). This is reproducible 100% of the time with clear repro steps and root cause identified, plus a suggested fix. Impact: affects a distinct but plausibly common subset of users (those using cluster mode Redis), with data loss (billing metrics) as a consequence, but there's no complete workaround mentioned by the reporter (other than avoiding cluster mode) and it deterministically breaks shutdown, causing data loss. This pushes toward P1 given the data-loss angle and clear reproduction, but affects only a subset (cluster-mode Redis users) — not "most users on a current release" but a fairly common configuration. Given the data loss and complete deterministic failure with no stated workaround, but restricted to a specific configuration, P2 seems appropriate as baseline, however the "data loss" impact plus complete shutdown breakage push this higher — but since it's not affecting most users only cluster-mode users, and there's no regression indicated, I'll set P2 given subset affected, no workaround stated, but not "broken for most users" threshold for P0/P1.
Since there's a clear reproduction, well-specified root cause and suggested fix already provided, this can be routed directly to the caching/redis module without further clarification — needs_human is false.

This is a well-documented architectural gap in the OAuth delegate/MCP server integration: when an upstream token grant has neither expires_in nor refresh_token, the gateway has no renewal path other than hourly full re-authorization, because the access envelope hits the 1h cap and no refresh envelope is minted. There's a workaround (repeat interactive auth) which is painful, which per feature-request classification doesn't independently raise urgency since features default to P3 with promotion only via evidenced multi-party demand. No regression, no multi-provider breadth signal beyond one report. So urgency = P3.

It affects a widely-used provider path (OpenAI gpt-5.4+ auto-bridged whenever reasoning + tools are used on /chat/completions), which is an increasingly common configuration for agentic workflows (LangChain/LangGraph clients), and there's no caller-side workaround since it's triggered automatically by responses_api_bridge_check() without any config change. Given many callers use OpenAI gpt-5.4+ with reasoning_effort and tools, and this is automatically triggered without opt-in, impact is broad across users hitting this code path (shared core bridging logic), though it's specific to one reasoning-capable model family and requires an automatic bridge trigger, so not "most users" broadly. A repro is given, is well-specified and confirmed in code inspection, with production evidence. There is no caller-facing workaround (since the bridging is automatic), but partial mitigation could be avoiding reasoning_effort + tools together, which is a stated modifier that could lower severity — however, this would break existing use cases. Given a widely-used provider (OpenAI) and shared core code path (Responses bridge) is affected and this can silently corrupt agent responses/break tool calling (already partially fixed by PR #33931 for the sibling case), I'll set urgency to P1: a major, widely used provider (OpenAI/gpt-5.4) integration is broken for common reasoning+tools usage without an easy workaround. Since this is P1, per rules this requires needs_human=true (judgement/reproduction confirmation, and it touches core bridging logic affecting many downstream integrations).

It doesn't rise to P0 since it's not a security issue affecting most users on all providers, but it affects a widely used provider path for tool calling scenarios and has no real workaround (client-side, they can't control how they normalize ids without proxy-side changes). The "many providers or shared core path" modifier could push it, but I'll settle at P1 given it's specific to Gemini/Vertex but a major provider and hard-fails ongoing sessions.

The reporter identifies that LiteLLM strips the `background` parameter when forwarding image generation requests for gpt-image-2 to OpenAI/Azure, whereas direct API calls correctly pass and honor it. This is behavior that does not exist yet (parameter pass-through support) — the code needs to support forwarding this param, which classifies it as a feature request for new parameter support, per the categorization guide ("new parameters or endpoints" -> feature). It's a single reporter with a clear, well-specified repro but no evidence of broader demand from multiple users, so default to P3. It's fairly well-specified (points to exact transformation files), so a maintainer could likely route/queue this without a back-and-forth discussion, but since it involves shared code paths for both OpenAI and Azure image generation transformations, there's some judgement around scope — however the specifics are clear enough to route directly to the owning module (gpt_transformation.py for both providers).

This is a clear regression/defect: LiteLLM's own openai-provider embedding code path force-injects an `encoding_format` default (float or base64 depending on env var) regardless of client input, and this default cannot be suppressed, causing 400 errors whenever the downstream provider (via a chained LiteLLM proxy) reports zero supported params for encoding_format. This breaks a documented/standard use case (two-hop LiteLLM proxy chaining over OpenAI-compatible surface) and violates expected behavior that omitting a field should not force a default value to be injected downstream. Code behaves differently from expected/documented behavior -> bug. It affects the shared embeddings path for any provider with no support for encoding_format behind an openai-provider hop, which is a widely-used chaining pattern, but the reporter demonstrates a clear reproduction and workaround (calling proxy B directly) exists, though not viable for the two-hop use case desired. Given a workaround exists (bypass proxy A) but this is core embeddings code affecting potentially many providers/chains, urgency is P1 due to shared core path impact, tempered by workaround availability lowering it to P2. This needs human review because it requires judgement to fix correctly across multiple related PRs/issues (linked churn) and confirm root cause interacts with several past fixes.

This is a well-articulated request for new functionality: a merge-safe metadata update API (PATCH/merge or CAS with revision) that does not currently exist. No existing behavior is documented as being violated—rather, the reporter is requesting a new safe management path/contract. This is a feature request, not a bug, since the code currently behaves as designed (whole-column replace), just without a safe merge mechanism. It's a single reporter (albeit detailed, cross-referencing a separate Terraform provider issue they also authored), so demand is not clearly corroborated by multiple independent parties within this repo. Per the rules, a detailed write-up alone does not count as evidenced demand, and a single requester defaults to P3. However, this does touch core user metadata handling and data-loss potential, which is a product-direction decision requiring maintainer judgement about API design (merge semantics, revision/ETag, deletion semantics), so needs_human should be true even though urgency is P3.

The issue reports that classifier cost, though recorded (classifier_cost), is not incorporated into the auto-router savings/benchmark rollup arithmetic, causing overstated savings and understated spend. This is a clear cost-accounting defect against the documented invariant (baseline_spend = spend + saved_spend), matching the "incorrect cost accounting" bug category explicitly called out in the rules. It's not a docs issue since the code's behavior violates the intended contract. It affects only users using LLM-based complexity routing with classifier cost tracking - a narrower path, not the core proxy request path, and a workaround (manual adjustment) is feasible, so it's not P0/P1. This is a well-specified, reproducible bug with a clear proof and suggested fix, so it can be routed without maintainer discussion.

This is a well-documented, reproducible bug in the core proxy client-caching/connection-pool lifecycle affecting all streaming providers (not just Anthropic) — the finalizer closes the shared httpx client out from under in-flight streams, killing all concurrent SSE streams hourly. This is the shared core path (client cache TTL/finalizer) so it affects many users broadly, not a narrow edge case. There's a clear root cause, reproduction steps, evidence from production (log clusters, error counts), a regression test, and a fix already up as a PR (#38242). Because the shared core connection-handling path is affected across all providers, and it causes silent data/turn loss for every concurrent user at the TTL boundary with no workaround (developers can't disable the TTL or avoid the eviction), this qualifies as very high impact — broken for most users with active streams on a current release, no workaround. That maps to P0, and since a fix is already proposed, this could arguably be routed without much debate, but given it's P0/P1-severity and touches core behavior, per rules P0/P1 issues need human judgement to confirm and merge. Category is bug: this is a violation of expected behavior (streams should not die due to internal cache housekeeping), not a feature request or docs issue.

The issue reports that RedisCache.test_connection() constructs a plain Redis client instead of using the Sentinel-aware runtime path, causing the admin test to fail even though real Sentinel operations succeed. This is a clear behavioral bug: documented/expected behavior is that the test should validate the actual connection path, but code takes a different path and produces false failures. There's also a secondary concern about redis-py 8.x compatibility via fragile constructor introspection, which is a real but more speculative/forward-looking risk (not yet manifesting in the pinned version). The core bug (test_connection bypassing Sentinel) is reproducible and specific with code references and evidence of failure, so it is a bug rather than a feature or question. It affects Sentinel users specifically (a subset of Redis users), and a workaround exists (rely on runtime behavior instead of the test, or pin redis-py 5.3.1), so urgency stays at P2 rather than higher. It doesn't affect most users (only Sentinel-configured deployments), and the redis-py 8.x issue is speculative/not yet triggered in the shipped version. Given the specificity of the code pointers and clear reproduction evidence, a maintainer could route this to the caching/redis module without much ambiguity, but the issue also bundles multiple asks (fix test_connection, add version constraints, CI tests, replace introspection) which suggests judgement is needed to decide scope of the fix — warranting human review.

This is a bug report describing incorrect/misleading warning logs at startup: (1) wildcard OpenRouter models are matched against a cost database as if they were specific models, (2) the same warning is emitted twice (once by name, once by id), and (3) the warning is spurious for providers like OpenRouter that report costs via response metadata, which litellm already ingests per prior PRs (#13653, #32255). The code's behavior (warning generation) diverges from the actual/intended cost-accounting logic already implemented elsewhere, so this fits "bug" rather than "docs" or "feature". It's not a security issue, and the author is reporting broken/misleading behavior rather than asking how to do something. Impact: affects any OpenRouter users using the wildcard-model dashboard feature — it's a warning/logging issue, not breaking core functionality, and there's no data loss or blocking crash. A workaround exists (ignore the warning), so it's a narrower, cosmetic-ish issue rather than P1. This affects an OpenRouter integration but only produces noisy logs, not broken behavior, so P2 seems too high; it's mostly cosmetic/log noise. Given it's confined to warning messages and doesn't break functionality, P3 is appropriate, but since it does touch shared cost-computation logic and affects clarity for many OpenRouter+wildcard users, P2 fits better upon reflection due to multiple related bugs bundled and core cost-check path affected. I'll go with P2.
Needs_human: true because this bundles three distinct sub-issues requiring judgement on how to fix (matching logic, dedup, provider-specific suppression), which is more than a trivial routing decision.

A stale import name (`indexDefinition` instead of `index_definition`) causes an unconditional ModuleNotFoundError at import time for any redis-py >= 5, which is essentially every currently installed version, including the official LiteLLM docker images. This makes the entire valkey-semantic cache backend completely unusable — a clear code defect vs. documented/expected behavior (bug, not docs, since the code itself is broken). There is a clear, well-understood one-line fix and reproduction steps provided, so a maintainer doesn't need to investigate further to understand the issue, though it should be verified before merging. Given it breaks a documented feature for all users on current releases with no workaround (other than pinning to redis-py 4.x, which is not a real workaround for most), this is high impact — P1. It's not P0 since it's a single narrower feature entirely broken, not core broken for most users, but it's also close to "widely-used provider" wide-impact since it affects every current redis-py install. Given the affected component (valkey-semantic cache) is not the shared core cache path (default caching type is different), P1 for a fully broken widely-affected feature is appropriate. No security concern applies. needs_human is set true because P1 severity triggers escalation policy, even though the fix is well-specified, to allow verification/PR review.

The user reports that adding a model with a Chinese-character name causes a real error when calling the model: "Error: 500 'latin-1' codec can't encode characters in position 0-1: ordinal not in range(256)". This is an actual encoding bug in the code (likely a header or HTTP encoding issue defaulting to latin-1) rather than a missing feature or docs issue—the software fails/crashes when a non-ASCII model name is used, which is an unexpected/incorrect behavior. Although labeled "Feature" and "Docs" by the reporter, the described behavior is a concrete error/crash, matching the bug category better than feature (this isn't about adding new capability, but fixing broken handling of valid input). This affects any user who names models with non-latin1 characters, which could be a global/core issue affecting the request pipeline. Given it's a specific reproducible bug affecting a subset of users (those using non-ASCII model names) with no clear workaround mentioned, but only reported by one user, urgency is moderate - P2. No evidence of regression or workaround. Needs human judgement to confirm reproduction and evaluate the root cause across providers, since encoding issues in headers could affect multiple providers.

This is a well-documented, evidenced bug report: pricing data in model_prices_and_context_window.json for many openrouter/* entries disagrees with OpenRouter's own published API/page prices, causing incorrect cost accounting for completion_cost(), proxy spend tracking, and budgets/alerts. This is "incorrect cost accounting" which per the rules is explicitly a bug category ("Provider X returns the wrong price" is a bug). It affects a widely-used shared path (cost calculation) across many providers/models (41 of 85 entries, spanning multiple provider families), which triggers the "many providers or shared core path affected → raise one level" modifier. Impact is broad (any spend tracking relying on openrouter pricing) though a workaround (manually overriding prices) exists, which would normally lower urgency by one level, but the widespread nature affecting core cost path pushes it to at least P1. Given the scale (41 entries wrong, affecting real billing/budget decisions) and no automated test catching this, it warrants prompt attention — P1. This requires a maintainer to verify the extensive claims and decide on a scoped fix/update process, so needs_human is true (per rules, "claims needing reproduction to confirm" and it's P1).

A synchronous, blocking device-code auth flow (with time.sleep loops up to 900s) is reachable from an async request handler with no await point. This blocks the entire event loop, starving health checks and all other in-flight requests on the same worker, leading to orchestrator-triggered container kills. This is a severe availability bug affecting all users of the proxy (not just chatgpt/* requests), with no workaround for a single-worker deployment, and it is triggerable by any valid key holder — effectively a DoS vector against the shared proxy. It behaves entirely differently from expected behavior (a request that cannot authenticate should fail fast), so this is a bug, not a feature or docs issue. Same defect pattern exists in github_copilot's authenticator, meaning multiple providers are affected via the shared request-handling path. Given it can take down the whole proxy for all users with no workaround, and is trivially repeatable by any user, this meets the bar for P0 (broken for most users on affected paths, no workaround, easily triggered denial of service). This requires maintainer judgement to decide the right architectural fix (thread offloading vs. refusing device flow when non-interactive) and to assess blast radius across two providers, so needs_human is true.
